title: Park Center Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Park Center wells have a 60-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling costs and water results vary widely.
intro_html:
Park Center sits in Fremont County’s mountain terrain, where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The local records show a 60-foot median well depth, but the full range is much wider: the deepest recorded well reaches 3,216 feet. Water production is generally stronger than many mountain areas, with an 11.0 gallons-per-minute median among wells reporting yield.

These records are useful for comparing nearby properties, not for guaranteeing what a new well will produce. Only 430 wells are recorded as constructed, 446 report total depth, 107 report pump yield, and 18 report static water level. Before buying land near Cañon City, Lincoln Park, Brookside or other nearby communities, review neighboring permits and have a driller evaluate the specific lot.

sections.heading: Park Center well depths reflect fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
Park Center wells are often shallow by Colorado mountain standards. The median recorded depth is 60 feet, and the middle half runs from 35 to 193 feet. About 65% are under 100 feet, while 16% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 13% from 300 to 600 feet, and 7% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 3,216 feet.

That spread matters when you ask for a drilling bid. A nearby shallow well may not predict your result because granite and gneiss can fracture differently from one lot to the next. Use nearby wells to establish a starting range, then ask a licensed driller how access, casing, grout and expected fractures could change the plan.

sections.heading: Most Park Center wells make usable household quantities
sections.html:
Among the 107 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 57% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 36% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% are under 1 gallon per minute, with 7% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a favorable local record, but it does not remove the risk of a low-yield or dry hole. Yield testing and storage design still matter, especially for a larger home, livestock or irrigation. An exempt household-use well remains subject to its permit terms and Colorado’s 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels do not cover enough wells for a trend
sections.html:
The 18 Park Center wells reporting static water level have a median depth to water of 62 feet. The middle half ranges from 16 to 154 feet. Those values help show how far a pump may need to lift water, but they are not a broad groundwater trend because static measurements are available for only a small part of the permitted record.

The permits identify 730 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, four in alluvial aquifers and three in the Dakota aquifer. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded. For a purchase, ask for the actual well test and static level on the property, then compare it with nearby permits rather than assuming the regional median applies to your lot.

sections.heading: Park Center drilling records span decades
sections.html:
Permit activity increased from five permits in the 1950s and nine in the 1960s to 50 in the 1970s, 75 in the 1980s, 106 in the 1990s and 176 in the 2000s. The record shows 92 permits in the 2010s and 69 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) and Young'S Drilling & Pump Serv (Young, Nolen). Permit history can show how nearby ground has been developed, but it is not a recommendation or proof that a contractor is available for your project. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope and references before signing.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost near Park Center
sections.html:
Park Center drilling is priced for fractured mountain bedrock, described in the local cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,900 to $6,000.

A finished system costs more than the hole. Including a pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, the modeled total is about $9,900 to $18,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or unexpected rock can move the bid higher. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space and building access
sections.html:
Environmental due diligence deserves attention around Park Center. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 76 historic mine features and four EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a particular well is contaminated, but they are good reasons to test the water and investigate the lot’s history, drainage and nearby land uses.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured rock even though the reported yield statistics are generally strong. Before building, confirm that the well location, septic system, replacement area, driveway and house site can fit together. Septic setbacks, trenching, steep access and electrical runs can affect both feasibility and cost. Water treatment should be based on laboratory results, not assumptions about mountain wells.

sections.heading: Use neighboring permits before buying a Park Center lot
sections.html:
Start with the permit map for the immediate property and nearby Cañon City, Lincoln Park, Brookside, Williamsburg and Rockvale records. Compare depths, reported yields and static water levels, paying attention to whether the neighboring wells are completed in similar fractured ground. The strongest evidence is usually the closest comparable well, not the regional median by itself.

For an existing home, obtain the well permit, construction record, pump information, recent flow test and water-quality results. For vacant land, make the drilling risk part of the purchase decision and ask a local driller to assess access and likely depth before closing. If the parcel is in an over-appropriated basin, confirm whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement applies before relying on a new well for the proposed use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Park Center, Colorado?
faq.a: Park Center wells have a 60-foot median recorded depth, with the middle half between 35 and 193 feet. About 65% are under 100 feet, but the range is broad in fractured mountain bedrock. The deepest recorded well is 3,216 feet, so nearby permits should be reviewed before estimating the depth for a specific lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Park Center?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 60-foot median depth, drilling alone is about $3,900 to $6,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $9,900 to $18,000. Difficult access or a deeper hole can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Park Center wells produce?
faq.a: Among 107 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 36% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded wells, not a guarantee for an un drilled location.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Park Center, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its test results. The area has 29 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 76 historic mine features and four EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those records do not establish contamination at your property. Test existing well water through a qualified laboratory and investigate nearby land uses before buying.

faq.q: Should I test a Park Center well before buying a home?
faq.a: Yes. Only 18 local wells report static water level, so regional figures cannot replace property records. Request the well permit, construction details, pump yield or flow test, static water level and recent laboratory results. Compare the property with nearby wells, especially because fractured-bedrock conditions can produce different depths and yields over short distances.
